title: My AI Adoption Journey
summary: Mitchell Hashimoto describes a staged, measured adoption of coding agents, built on verification tools, harness engineering and background agents.

assertions.quote: To find value, you must use an agent.
The command palette that ships for macOS in Ghostty today is only very lightly modified from what Gemini produced for me in seconds.
I forced myself to reproduce all my manual commits with agentic ones.
For vague requests, split the work into separate planning vs. execution sessions.
If you give an agent a way to verify its work, it more often than not fixes its own mistakes and prevents regressions.
anytime you find an agent makes a mistake, you take the time to engineer a solution such that the agent never makes that mistake again.
Each line in that file is based on a bad agent behavior, and it almost completely resolved them all.
instead of trying to do more in the time I have, try to do more in the time I don't have.
Deep research sessions where I'd ask agents to survey some field
I'm not [yet?] running multiple agents, and currently don't really want to.
not forming skills for the tasks you're delegating to the agent
the latter part of the working day, I'm usually tired and coming out of flow and find myself too personally inefficient

verdicts.note: This fits METR's finding of lower perceived effort and practitioner reports, but it has not been directly measured.

METR RCT: reports on effort were mixed ('felt like less effort' vs 'no effort difference'), and 69% kept using Cursor despite the measured slowdown. That hints at lower cognitive load, but tired or distracted work was not studied.
